name: The AI Enablement Audit
title: The AI Enablement Audit
answer: The AI Enablement Audit is the review an organisation runs to establish what artificial intelligence it actually uses, who can reach it, and what data flows through it. It sits between a security audit and an adoption programme, because its purpose is to make sanctioned use easier while closing off the shadow use that grows when staff adopt tools without telling anyone. In practice it covers employee accounts on hosted assistants, embedded features inside existing software, internal models, and the spreadsheets and scripts that quietly call a model API. The output is a register of systems, owners, data categories and access paths rather than a pass or fail verdict.

AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit is the review an organisation runs to establish what artificial intelligence it actually uses, who can reach it, and what data flows through it. It sits between a security audit and an adoption programme, because its purpose is to make sanctioned use easier while closing off the shadow use that grows when staff adopt tools without telling anyone. In practice it covers employee accounts on hosted assistants, embedded features inside existing software, internal models, and the spreadsheets and scripts that quietly call a model API. The output is a register of systems, owners, data categories and access paths rather than a pass or fail verdict.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same inventory and identity material the organisation already holds: single sign on logs, software asset records, procurement and expense data, cloud billing, network egress records and endpoint agents. Browser extensions and personal accounts are the usual blind spots, so discovery often combines a network or proxy view with a short self reporting survey. Larger estates add a data catalogue and a model or prompt registry to link each tool to the information it can touch. The site's catalogue of 850 AI tools is the kind of reference list an auditor uses to recognise a product name found in a log.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with discovery, then moves to classification of each tool by data sensitivity, user population and vendor terms, and then to a decision on whether to approve, restrict or retire it. Evidence is gathered from configuration exports, contract terms, vendor documentation and interviews with the teams that bought or built the tool. Findings are recorded against a control set so that the same questions can be asked again next quarter, and remediation is tracked as ordinary IT and legal work rather than as a separate programme. The audit is repeated on a cycle because new tools appear continuously and old approvals go stale.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The audit is where contractual, regulatory and litigation exposure meet, so legal, security, privacy and procurement all read the same register. Vendor terms decide whether inputs may be used for training, where data is stored, what happens on termination, and whether the supplier will support a subject access request or a deletion demand. Intellectual property is the dominant concern in current disputes, and the site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, alongside 29 case law precedents and 229 compliance and regulation pages. Records of what was deployed, when, and on whose authority are what make an incident answerable later, and 7166 state AI bills show how much of the surrounding rule making is still in motion.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from an annual project to a standing control, with discovery automated through identity and network tooling and approvals issued as short lived entitlements rather than permanent purchases. Registers will increasingly record model versions and prompt changes, not just product names, because a tool that was reviewed once can behave differently after an update. Vendor attestations and standard contract terms will carry more of the load as buyers refuse to review each supplier from scratch. The open question is staffing, since the same small team is usually asked to run discovery, contract review and incident response at the same time.
